lesson.title: Perfect Tense Gym
lesson.subtitle: gewerkt, gemaakt, gekomen, gegaan — build the participle and choose the helper

hook.title: Two Halves, One Past
hook.content: Every perfect sentence has the same two halves: helper first, participle last. Ik heb het gemaakt, wij zijn gegaan, hij is gebleven. The order is a bracket.

pattern.title: Helper second, participle last
pattern.content: In a main clause the helper is the finite verb in second place; the participle closes the sentence. Ik heb gewerkt, wij zijn gegaan, zij is gekomen.
pattern.trap_note: Do not put the participle before the helper in a main clause: ik gewerkt heb is subordinate-clause order, not main-clause order.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Perfect Tense Gym):
exercises.target_answer: hebben, zijn, blijven, gaan, komen, maken
exercises.meaning: to have, to be, to stay, to go, to come, to make
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Perfect Tense Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik ben gebleven.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Perfect Tense Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Helper second, participle last
exercises.explanation: “Wij zijn gegaan.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Helper second, participle last.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not put the participle before the helper in a main clause: ik gewerkt heb is subordinate-clause order, not main-clause order.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Hij heeft gewerkt.” is word-for-word “He has worked.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Helper second, participle last.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Zij is gekomen.” reuses only material taught in “Perfect Tense Gym” — Helper second, participle last.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Zij is gekomen.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Helper second, participle last.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I have made it.”
twist.explanation: Maken takes hebben; the participle gemaakt closes the sentence.

summary.outcome: Keep the perfect bracket in the right order in main clauses.
summary.takeaway: The perfect is a bracket: helper second, participle last.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The Future & the Would-World.

hebben.etymology_derivation: English have and Dutch hebben descend from the same verb; the b is preserved.

zijn.etymology_derivation: The being verb is irregular in every Germanic language; English is and Dutch is are the same old root.

blijven.etymology_derivation: English stay is a different verb; Dutch blijven is the direct Germanic twin of German bleiben.

gaan.etymology_derivation: The same verb as English go, with the old g still pronounced.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

maken.etymology_derivation: English make and Dutch maken are the same verb; German shifted k to ch in machen.
